top.line: A proposed aws.twin.sgit.ai: a twin on a vault first, then a temporary AWS session in front of it.
top.para: Building AWS tools on the client lacked a place for the credentials and a place for the data; the vault gives both. aws.twin.sgit.ai is a twin first: an AWS-shaped interface on a vault, with the live account as a second backend. Temporary credentials from the access portal go into a vault, the browser calls AWS, and results go back as snapshots.

in-short.line: Credentials in the vault, a twin first, the browser does the work, data in the vault.
in-short.para: A client-side site for managing AWS, at aws.twin.sgit.ai. Built on a vault first, with the live account as a second backend. Credentials come from the AWS access portal and last one to twelve hours. The browser uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript; the vault holds the results. First job: multi-region deployment. IAM Roles Anywhere may give a PKI route.

missing.line: Years of AWS tooling, and two missing pieces: where the credentials and the data go.
missing.para: OSBot-AWS, an Apache 2.0 Python library with about 1,180 commits, and SG/Compute, which launches and terminates EC2 environments, took the code a long way. What was missing was a safe place in the browser for an AWS session, and somewhere to keep what it gathers. The user's vault answers both.

twin.line: A twin first: an AWS-shaped interface on a vault, with the live account as a second backend.
twin.para: The site is aws.twin.sgit.ai, in the twins family. It is built as an AWS-shaped interface whose backend is a vault, with the temporary session put in front as a second backend behind the same interface, the pattern of the working S3 container twin. Everything can be built and tested with no credentials, and deployments rehearsed before running live.

workflow.line: Sign in to the AWS access portal, copy temporary credentials, paste them into the vault.
workflow.para: IAM Identity Center grants temporary credentials, which AWS recommends over long-term ones. Pick an account and permission set, choose Access keys, and paste the access key, secret key and session token into a vault, which can be temporary. Sessions last one to twelve hours, one by default. Copying by hand keeps the site to one short session.

browser.line: The browser does the work with the AWS SDK for JavaScript; CORS is the first test.
browser.para: With the session in the vault, the site can browse S3, see Lambda functions and EC2 instances, read billing, map IAM and gather logs, with workflows built one at a time. S3 buckets need CORS configured, and other services use CORS too, so which answer a browser must be measured; a local helper or an SG/Compute node can cover the rest.

data.line: The vault is where AWS data goes: versioned snapshots that become graphs.
data.para: Inventories, costs and logs go back into the vault, each snapshot a commit, so changes between two days can be seen. Resources become nodes and their links become edges, which asks of an AWS account what this site asks of agents: what can reach what. The graph is built from the source and read as slices and diffs.

deploy.line: The first job: deploying the SG/Send server components to many regions and accounts.
deploy.para: The templates exist, for Lambda as a container image with a function URL and for ECS Fargate, with an S3 storage mode and runbooks for new accounts and regions. With one session per account, the site can run a template into each region and record every deployment in the vault, which becomes the record of the estate.

pki.line: IAM Roles Anywhere exchanges X.509 certificates for temporary credentials; to test.
pki.para: AWS's IAM Roles Anywhere lets workloads outside AWS get temporary credentials with certificates from your own certificate authority, registered as a trust anchor. It fits the PKI everywhere direction. Whether it can work from a browser, with a non-exportable key, and whether its endpoint answers a browser, is to test. Its resources are regional.

careful.line: Narrow roles, short sessions, versioned site code, and no credentials in pages.
careful.para: A session can do whatever its role can, so roles should be narrow and sessions short. The site's code holds the session, so it should be released as fixed, independent versions. AWS advises against hard-coding credentials in browser code; here they are pasted per session and kept in the vault. Some calls may need a helper.

limits.line: The name is decided; nothing is built; browser access and Roles Anywhere are untested.
limits.para: aws.twin.sgit.ai is decided and its repository exists; the site does not. S3 needs CORS and other services are still to measure. IAM Roles Anywhere from a browser is untested. The deployment templates are written but not a reviewed reference architecture. AWS is quoted from its documentation, read on 21 October 2026.

diagrams.line: The Mermaid source of both diagrams, to reuse or correct.
diagrams.para: The flow from the AWS access portal through the vault to aws.twin.sgit.ai in the browser, AWS, and back into the vault, and the example deployment of one template through two account sessions into several regions, as Mermaid source.

sources.line: A voice memo, AWS documentation, OSBot-AWS, SG/Compute, twins.sgit.ai and sgit.ai's AWS page.
sources.para: A voice memo of 21 October 2026; AWS's pages on IAM Identity Center credentials, IAM Roles Anywhere, and the SDK for JavaScript on CORS and browser credentials; OSBot-AWS on GitHub; SG/Compute's site; twins.sgit.ai on the S3 container; and sgit.ai's AWS page, with related newsroom articles.
